[THOUGHT] Clinical reasoning:

Key unifying findings: profound plasmacytosis in bone marrow (80% plasma cells) with IgG-κ monoclonal protein on immunofixation, hypercalcemia (11.5 mg/dL) and acute kidney injury (Cr 5.6 mg/dL) — these meet criteria for symptomatic plasma cell myeloma. Peripheral smear shows rouleaux and cryoprotein precipitate, and cryocrit is 16% with instructions to keep viscosity specimen warm — all pointing to clinically significant monoclonal cryoglobulinemia (type I) with heavy circulating paraprotein. The patient has purpuric skin lesions with a normal platelet count, which argues against thrombocytopenia and instead favors purpura from vascular occlusion/ischemia or cryoglobulin-associated small-vessel injury. Other causes of purpura/vasculitis (immune complex cryoglobulinemia type II/III, ANCA-associated vasculitis) or other monoclonal-protein disorders that cause hyperviscosity (e.g., Waldenström macroglobulinemia) are less likely given the IgG-κ monoclonal protein and marrow findings.

4. Myeloma-associated renal disease (light-chain/cast nephropathy or monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance) explaining the acute kidney injury.

5. Cryoglobulinemic small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis related to the monoclonal protein (less likely as a separate primary process but plausible mechanism for the purpura).
